items.title: Level 5: Invitation problems and what to do about them
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Real life does not always match the neat steps in a guide, so it helps to practise handling problems with the invitation. Suppose the invitation gives a date when you cannot attend, perhaps because of a hospital appointment or a clash with a childcare commitment. Contact the recruitment team straight away, using the details in the invitation, and give a brief reason. Many teams can offer another slot, especially for good reasons, but they cannot always do so, and the sooner you ask, the better your chances. Suppose the invitation does not say which format will be used, or the link does not appear. Do not guess. Email or phone the named contact and ask. Suppose you need an adjustment, such as extra time or a quiet room, and the invitation does not mention it. Ask for it in writing, early, and keep a copy of the reply. Suppose the invitation asks for identity documents. Check which ones are acceptable, and if you have difficulty producing any, ask what alternatives exist before the day. Suppose you receive a second invitation for the same job. Check the dates carefully and reply to the most recent one, asking if unsure. Suppose you spot an error, such as the wrong job title or a date that has already passed. Query it politely at once instead of assuming. Suppose you have been invited to two interviews on the same day. Tell both teams, as one may be able to move. Finally, whatever happens, keep copies of all your messages, so you can show what was agreed.

questions.prompt: Your interview date clashes with a hospital appointment. What is the best first step?

options.text: Wait to see whether the date can be changed on the day
Keep the appointment and rebook the interview yourself afterwards
Contact the recruitment team straight away with a brief reason
Ask a friend to explain your absence to the panel

questions.hint: Early contact gives the team the best chance to find another slot.

questions.prompt: The invitation does not say whether the interview is by video or in person. What should you do?

options.text: Go to the department's main office to find out
Prepare for video and hope that is right
Email or phone the named contact to ask
Check the format on the panel members' professional profiles

questions.hint: Do not guess; ask the contact in the invitation.

questions.prompt: You need extra time but the invitation does not mention adjustments. What is the sensible way to ask?

options.text: By mentioning it in your reply to the offer
By telling the panel at the start of the interview
In writing and early, keeping a copy of the reply
By phoning on the morning of the interview

questions.hint: Asking early in writing gives time to arrange and a record to refer to.

questions.prompt: The invitation asks for identity documents and you cannot provide one of them. What should you do?

options.text: Ask a friend to confirm who you are
Say nothing and hope that it will not be checked
Bring whatever documents you have and explain on the day
Ask before the day which alternatives are acceptable

questions.hint: Query the requirement early rather than risk problems on the day.

questions.prompt: The invitation gives the wrong job title. What is the best response?

options.text: Reply using the title you believe is correct
Assume it is a typing error and ignore it
Wait until the interview to mention it
Politely query it at once

questions.hint: A prompt query avoids confusion.

questions.prompt: You are invited to two interviews on the same day. What is a sensible approach?

options.text: Choose one and let the other invitation lapse
Ask one team to cancel the other for you
Tell both teams so that one may be able to move
Attend the first interview and rush to the second

questions.hint: Telling both teams gives them a chance to help.

questions.prompt: You receive a second invitation for the same job with a different date. What should you do?

options.text: Wait for a third message to confirm which is correct
Attend the earlier date, since you accepted it first
Attend both dates in case one is a mistake
Reply to the most recent one, asking if unsure

questions.hint: Use the most recent invitation and ask if unclear.

questions.prompt: Why keep copies of all your messages with the recruitment team?

options.text: So that you can send them on to other applicants
So that you can show what was agreed
So that you can attach them to your application
So that the panel can read them before the interview

questions.hint: Copies give a record of agreements.

questions.prompt: The meeting link does not work thirty minutes before the interview. What is the best action?

options.text: Phone the named contact in the invitation
Message the panel members directly on social media
Wait until the start time and then try the link again
Cancel and ask to be rescheduled

questions.hint: Use the contact number straight away.

questions.prompt: You are asked for a reason when you request a change of date. How should you respond?

options.text: Offer a different reason that sounds more convincing
Give a long explanation covering all your circumstances
Give a brief, honest reason without unnecessary detail
Decline to give any reason

questions.hint: A short honest reason is enough.

items.title: Level 5: Matching your examples to the questions
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Preparation is useful only if you can pick the right example in the moment. Imagine you have five prepared stories: helping a new colleague in a shop, clearing a backlog of mail in a school office, calming an angry customer at a till, organising a family member's appointments, and working on a group project at college. Now consider how you would choose when asked questions. For 'Tell us about a time you had to meet a tight deadline', the mail backlog fits well because it involves planning and time pressure. For 'Tell us about a time you dealt with a difficult person', the angry customer is the natural choice. For 'Tell us about a time you helped someone to learn', the new colleague story is best. For 'Tell us about a time you worked as part of a team to achieve something', the college project works, though the shop story might also fit. For 'Tell us about a time you showed attention to detail', the appointments story could work, since errors there matter. The skill is to read the question, scan your list quickly and choose the story where your own actions most clearly match. If two stories fit, choose the one you remember best. If you used one story earlier in the interview, avoid using it again unless you have no alternative. If you realise halfway through that you picked the wrong story, say so and switch. A short list of headlines, such as 'mail backlog: deadline, planning', written on a card, can help you to choose quickly.

questions.prompt: Which prepared story best answers 'Tell us about a time you had to meet a tight deadline'?

options.text: Working on a college group project
Helping a new colleague in a shop
Clearing the mail backlog in a school office
Calming an angry customer at a busy till

questions.hint: The mail backlog involved planning and time pressure.

questions.prompt: Which prepared story best answers 'Tell us about a time you dealt with a difficult person'?

options.text: Clearing a backlog of mail in an office
Helping a new colleague learn a system
Calming an angry customer at a till
Organising a relative's appointments

questions.hint: The angry customer story shows handling difficulty.

questions.prompt: Which prepared story best answers 'Tell us about a time you helped someone to learn'?

options.text: Calming an angry customer at a till
Clearing the mail backlog in an office
Helping a new colleague in a shop
Working on a college group project

questions.hint: Helping a colleague learn is the closest match.

questions.prompt: Which prepared story could best show attention to detail?

options.text: Calming an angry customer at a busy till
Helping a new colleague settle into a shop
Working on a college group project with classmates
Organising a relative's appointments

questions.hint: Appointments involve accuracy.

questions.prompt: Two of your stories fit a question. How should you choose between them?

options.text: Pick the one with the most dramatic result
Pick the one that happened most recently
Pick the one that took the longest
Pick the one you remember best

questions.hint: A well-remembered story survives probing.

questions.prompt: You have already used the shop story earlier in the interview. What is the best approach for a later question that it also fits?

options.text: Use the shop story again with new detail
Combine the shop story with a different one
Say it was already covered and skip the question
Use another story unless you have no alternative

questions.hint: Reusing a story can look as if you have little to offer.

questions.prompt: Halfway through an answer you realise you picked the wrong story. What should you do?

options.text: Carry on and finish the story
Stop and ask to return to it later
Say so and switch to a better example
Blend in details from another story

questions.hint: Switching openly is better than forcing a poor fit.

questions.prompt: What is a quick way to choose a story under pressure?

options.text: Read each story silently at the start
Ask the panel for a hint about what they want
Keep a card of short headlines for each story
Keep a card with each story written in full

questions.hint: Headlines help recall quickly.

questions.prompt: A question asks about achieving something in a team. Which story fits, though others might too?

options.text: Calming an angry customer on your own
The college group project
Organising a relative's appointments alone
Clearing the mail backlog by yourself

questions.hint: The group project involved teamwork.

questions.prompt: What is the main skill when matching stories to questions?

options.text: Choosing the story that is most recent
Choosing the story with the most people involved
Choosing the story where your own actions most clearly fit
Choosing the story with the most impressive outcome

questions.hint: Fit with the question matters most.

items.title: Level 5: Repairing a weak answer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Being able to repair an answer on the spot is a practical skill. Suppose a candidate is asked, 'Tell us about a time you worked under pressure.' They begin: 'In my last job it was always busy and I think I coped well. We had a lot of customers and not many staff.' After a few sentences they realise they have said nothing specific. The best move is to pause and anchor the answer in one event. They might say, 'Let me give you a specific example. Last December, two colleagues were off sick on the same day...' and then move into the Situation, Task, Action and Result. Another weak pattern is the answer that goes quiet in the middle. If you lose your thread, glance at your notes if they are allowed, or say, 'Let me pick that up,' and return to the last point. A third pattern is the answer without a result. If you finish the actions and the panel waits, add, 'The outcome was...' straight away. A fourth is the answer that says 'we' throughout. If you notice, you can say, 'My part in this was...' and then describe what you personally did. A fifth is giving too much background. If you realise you have spoken for a minute without reaching your own role, say, 'To get to my part...' and move on. Repairs like these are normal, and panels respect them because they show awareness. It is better to adjust quickly than to carry on with an answer you know is going wrong.

questions.prompt: A candidate starts 'In my last job it was always busy and I think I coped well.' What is the best repair?

options.text: Move to a strengths answer instead
Carry on describing the general feel of the job
Ask the panel whether that answers the question
Pause and anchor the answer in one specific event

questions.hint: A specific event gives the panel something to score.

questions.prompt: You lose your thread in the middle of an answer. What is a sensible move?

options.text: Stop and move on to a different question
Ask the panel to remind you what you said
Start the answer again from the very beginning
Glance at notes if allowed, then return to your last point

questions.hint: Acknowledge the pause and return to the last point.

questions.prompt: You finish describing your actions and the panel waits. What should you add?

options.text: The outcome
An apology for the delay
A new story
Another action

questions.hint: The panel needs the Result.

questions.prompt: You notice you have said 'we' throughout. Which repair works?

options.text: 'Everyone did their bit, so we all deserve credit.'
'I will now talk about the team's work.'
'I was not involved in the details.'
'My part in this was...' and what you did

questions.hint: Reclaim your actions with 'my part'.

questions.prompt: You have spoken for a minute about background without reaching your own role. What is the best move?

options.text: Ask whether the panel wants more background
Say 'To get to my part...' and move on
Start the story again with less detail
Finish the background and then stop

questions.hint: Move to your actions quickly.

questions.prompt: Why do panels respect a quick repair?

options.text: It shows you can speak at length
It shows awareness and control
It shows you have lost confidence
It shows you did not prepare

questions.hint: Self-correction demonstrates awareness.

questions.prompt: Which opening makes a vague answer specific?

options.text: 'It is hard to give one example because...'
'Let me give you a specific example. Last December...'
'People say that I cope well under pressure.'
'In general, I usually find that...'

questions.hint: Naming a time anchors the story.

questions.prompt: After a weak start, what is better than carrying on regardless?

options.text: Saying that you were nervous
Finishing the answer as planned
Asking to skip the question
Adjusting quickly

questions.hint: Early repair saves the answer.

questions.prompt: A candidate forgets to mention the result in an otherwise good answer. When is it still fine to add it?

options.text: At the end of the whole interview
Not at all, once the answer has ended
Only if the panel asks directly
Straight after the actions, or when the panel pauses

questions.hint: Adding the outcome as soon as you notice is fine.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows a good attitude to repairing answers?

options.text: Repairs should be avoided at all costs
Any mistake means the answer will score nothing
Quick adjustments are normal and show awareness
Repairs are allowed only once per interview

questions.hint: Panels respect calm repairs.

items.title: Level 5: Video interview emergencies
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Here are realistic emergencies in video interviews and sensible responses. If your internet drops completely, rejoin straight away if you can. If you cannot, phone the number in the invitation and explain; many teams will rearrange or give you a short time to reconnect, but you will only get help if you contact them quickly. If your device battery dies, use your charger and rejoin, and keep a second charger within reach to avoid this in the first place. If your microphone stops working, check the platform's settings, then try the phone's audio or a different headset. If this takes more than a minute, tell the panel by chat or phone. If the panel's connection is poor, do not blame them. Politely ask if they can hear you, and offer to repeat. If a family member walks in, apologise briefly and continue. If the platform asks you to download software at the last minute, follow the instructions in the invitation, but if it is not mentioned, contact the team. If you accidentally mute yourself, a quick 'Sorry, I was on mute' is enough. If you notice that your notes are visible on a shared screen, close them. Do not use another device to look up answers, as it is dishonest and likely to be noticed. If the panel asks you to move to your phone because of problems, do so without fuss. Afterward, keep a note of what went wrong, as you may need to explain it if your performance was affected.

questions.prompt: Your internet drops completely mid-interview. What is the best first response?

options.text: Rejoin quickly, then phone the invitation number if you cannot
Wait quietly for the panel to contact you
Send the panel a message on social media
Restart your computer and take as long as you need

questions.hint: Quick rejoin then phone is best.

questions.prompt: Your device battery dies. What is the best response?

options.text: Wait for the panel to call you back
Plug in the charger and rejoin as quickly as you can
Switch to a friend's phone without telling the panel
Email the panel an apology the next day

questions.hint: Rejoin quickly and keep a spare charger to hand.

questions.prompt: Your microphone stops working. What is the first sensible step?

options.text: Check the platform's audio settings
End the call and rejoin later
Ask the panel to turn up their volume
Speak louder so they can hear you

questions.hint: Settings are the first thing to check.

questions.prompt: If a microphone problem takes more than a minute to fix, what should you do?

options.text: Keep trying silently until it works
Tell the panel by chat or phone
Switch off your camera to save bandwidth
Wait for the panel to notice

questions.hint: Keep the panel informed.

questions.prompt: The panel's connection is poor and you cannot hear them clearly. What is the best approach?

options.text: Pretend you heard and give a general answer
Switch off your camera to save bandwidth
Tell them their connection is poor and ask them to fix it
Politely check that they can hear you and offer to repeat

questions.hint: Stay polite and helpful.

questions.prompt: A family member walks into the room during your answer. What should you do?

options.text: End the call and ask to rebook
Ignore it without comment
Stop and explain the situation in detail
Apologise briefly and continue

questions.hint: A brief apology is enough.

questions.prompt: You accidentally mute yourself while answering. What is the best response?

options.text: 'Sorry, I was on mute' and repeat the last point
Finish the answer in the hope it was heard
Wait for the panel to tell you
Carry on talking in silence until they react

questions.hint: A quick apology and repeat is enough.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to use another device to look up answers?

options.text: It makes your notes harder to read
It is allowed only for strengths questions
It uses too much battery
It is dishonest and likely to be noticed

questions.hint: Looking up answers is dishonest.

questions.prompt: The panel asks you to move to your phone because of problems. How should you respond?

options.text: Do so calmly and without fuss
Insist on staying on the computer
Say you cannot manage with a phone
Ask the panel to rebook instead

questions.hint: Be cooperative.

questions.prompt: Why keep a note of what went wrong in a video emergency?

options.text: You can use it as an example in later interviews
You may need to explain it if your performance suffered
The panel will ask for a written report afterwards
It is required before feedback can be given

questions.hint: A record helps if you need to ask for consideration.

items.title: Level 5: Difficult moments with the panel
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Interviews do not always go smoothly, and the panel may do things that unsettle you. Suppose a panel member does not smile, looks at their notes and gives no reaction. This is normal. They are trained to stay neutral and they are writing evidence. Keep going. Suppose a panel member interrupts you to ask a follow-up. Stop politely and answer. Interruptions are usually to keep to time or to probe a point. Suppose the panel seems to be rushing through the questions. Pace yourself as normal. Do not speed up. If you feel you have not had a chance to show something, you can say, 'May I add one thing?' near the end, if time allows. Suppose a panel member asks a question that seems personal or unrelated to the job, such as about your family plans or your health. You are not required to answer questions that are not relevant, and such questions may be unfair. You can say politely, 'I'm not sure how that relates to the role, but I can tell you about my availability.' If you are worried, you can raise it afterwards with the recruitment team. Suppose someone on the panel appears to know you. Tell the host at the start, as this must be declared. Suppose a panel member makes a mistake, such as using the wrong name. Politely correct them without fuss. Suppose a question is repeated in different words. Do not assume you did badly; they may be seeking a specific aspect. Stay calm, courteous and clear throughout.

questions.prompt: A panel member looks down at their notes and shows no reaction as you answer. What is the best response?

options.text: Keep going calmly, as they are taking notes
Pause and ask whether the answer is what they wanted
Stop and check that they are still listening to you
Speed up so that you keep their attention

questions.hint: Neutral faces are normal because panels are trained not to react.

questions.prompt: A panel member interrupts you with a follow-up question part-way through an answer. What should you do?

options.text: Stop politely and answer the question they have asked
Carry on and deal with the question at the end
Finish your sentence and the point you were making first
Ask them to hold the question until you have finished

questions.hint: Interruptions are often to probe a point or keep to time.

questions.prompt: The panel seems to be rushing through the questions. What is the best approach?

options.text: Speed up your answers to match the panel's speed
Ask the panel to slow down before the next question
Keep to your normal pace and give full answers
Slow right down so the panel is forced to follow you

questions.hint: Keep your own steady pace.

questions.prompt: Near the end you feel you have not shown something important. What can you ask?

options.text: 'May I add one thing before we finish?'
'Could we go back and start that answer again?'
'Was that enough for me to get a good score?'
'Could I rewrite one of my earlier answers?'

questions.hint: A short request to add a point is acceptable if time allows.

questions.prompt: A panel member asks about your family plans. What is a sensible response?

options.text: Say politely it is unclear how it relates to the role
Ask them why they have asked and wait for an explanation
Say nothing and refuse to answer any further questions
Answer in full so that you do not seem unco-operative

questions.hint: You need not answer questions that are not relevant to the job.

questions.prompt: If you are worried about an inappropriate question, what can you do afterwards?

options.text: Leave it, because it cannot be reported
Raise it with the recruitment team
Mention it in a review on a jobs website
Write to the panel member who asked it

questions.hint: The recruitment team can look into it.

questions.prompt: You realise at the start that someone on the panel knows you personally. What should you do?

options.text: Mention it casually during your first answer
Carry on and mention it in your feedback
Say nothing, as the panel will sort it out themselves
Tell the host straight away so it can be declared

questions.hint: Possible conflicts of interest must be declared at the start.

questions.prompt: A panel member uses the wrong name for you. What is the best response?

options.text: Politely correct them without fuss
Use the wrong name in return to be polite
Say nothing and answer as if it were your name
Correct them at the end of the interview only

questions.hint: A polite correction is fine.

questions.prompt: A question is repeated in different words. How should you interpret this?

options.text: The panel expects you to repeat the same answer
The panel may want a particular aspect, so answer calmly
The panel has forgotten they already asked it
Your answer was poor and you should simply move on

questions.hint: Rephrasing is often a prompt to cover a missing aspect.

questions.prompt: Which attitude helps most when the interview becomes difficult?

options.text: Quiet, passive and apologetic
Firm, argumentative and persistent
Calm, courteous and clear
Quick, defensive and detailed

questions.hint: Calm courtesy keeps you in control.

items.title: Level 5: Blanking and recovering in practice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Imagine you are asked 'Tell us about a time you improved a process' and your mind goes blank. A calm routine can help. First, take a breath and say, 'That is a good question. Could I take a moment to think?' Then use the time to scan the headlines on your list. Ask yourself three quick questions: have I ever noticed something that could be done better? Did I suggest a change? Did anyone benefit? Often a small example emerges, such as rearranging a stockroom, creating a checklist or suggesting a different rota. If nothing comes, say, 'I'm struggling to find the right example for that one. May I come back to it at the end?' Many panels will agree. If they do not, you can give an example that only partly fits and say so honestly, or explain how you would approach it in that situation. Do not invent a story. Another useful tactic is to repeat the question aloud, which can jog your memory and buys a few seconds. If you start an example and it goes badly, you can stop and say, 'Let me start again.' After a blank, do not apologise repeatedly. Move to the next question with fresh energy, because each question is scored separately. A weak score on one is not fatal. The panel will remember how you recovered. Practise by asking a friend to throw you unexpected questions, and train yourself to stay calm.

questions.prompt: You blank on 'Tell us about a time you improved a process'. What is the best first step?

options.text: Ask the panel to move on to another question
Say that you have never improved anything
Start talking and hope that an example arrives
Take a breath and ask for a moment to think

questions.hint: A short pause is accepted.

questions.prompt: Which quick question might help you find an example of improving a process?

options.text: Which process is the department most proud of?
Did I ever notice something that could be done better?
Which of my examples has the best ending?
Which process would the panel like me to change?

questions.hint: Think of small improvements you suggested or made.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a small but valid example of improving a process?

options.text: Reading a book about how to improve processes
Watching a colleague improve a process
Creating a checklist for a task you did at work
Complaining that a process was too slow

questions.hint: A checklist you made is a real improvement.

questions.prompt: If nothing comes after a pause, what can you ask?

options.text: 'May I come back to this one at the end?'
'Could we skip the rest of the questions?'
'Is this question compulsory for the job?'
'Could you give me an example to start me off?'

questions.hint: Many panels will agree to return to a question.

questions.prompt: If the panel does not agree to return later, what is an honest option?

options.text: Say that you would rather not answer this one
Repeat an example you used for an earlier question
Give a partly fitting example and say so
Invent an example that fits the question exactly

questions.hint: Honesty is better than invention.

questions.prompt: How can repeating the question aloud help when you blank?

options.text: It can jog your memory and buys a few seconds
It shows the panel that your voice is steady
It counts towards your answer in the scoring
It lets the panel hear the question a second time

questions.hint: Repetition gives thinking time.

questions.prompt: You start an example and it is clearly going badly. What can you say?

options.text: 'Please ignore what I have just said'
'I will stop here, if that is all right'
'This is not going very well for me'
'Let me start again with a better example'

questions.hint: A polite restart is acceptable.

questions.prompt: After a blank, what is the best attitude to the next question?

options.text: Move on afresh, as each question is scored separately
Apologise to the panel and explain how nervous you are
Try to make up the lost marks with a longer next answer
Take it easy, since the marks for this round are gone

questions.hint: Each question stands alone.

questions.prompt: What is the panel most likely to remember about a blank?

options.text: How you recovered
That you blanked
How long it lasted
Which question caused it

questions.hint: Recovery shows resilience.

questions.prompt: How can you practise for the possibility of blanking?

options.text: Read the advert more times before the day
Memorise answers to every question you can imagine
Ask a friend to ask you unexpected questions
Avoid practising the questions you find hardest

questions.hint: Unexpected questions build calm under pressure.

items.title: Level 5: Judging strengths answers in practice
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Strengths questions are quick, so it helps to practise judging answers. Take the question 'What do you do when you have too much to do?' Candidate One says: 'I make a list, work out what is most urgent and tick things off. I like seeing the list shrink.' Candidate Two says: 'I stay calm and get everything done.' Candidate One's answer is stronger because it is specific, honest and shows enjoyment. Candidate Two makes a claim but does not show how. Now take 'Are you more of a planner or a doer?' Candidate A says: 'I'm a planner, always, and I get frustrated by people who do not plan.' Candidate B says: 'I like to plan, but I am happy to start and adjust as I go, particularly when a customer needs help right away.' B is stronger because it shows flexibility and consideration of others. A shows rigidity and a negative view of colleagues. Another example is 'What are you proud of?' A good answer is brief and real: 'Helping my nephew learn to read. He struggled, and when he finished his first book I felt very proud.' Weak answers boast or are vague. When you answer strengths questions, listen for what the question is really exploring. 'How do you feel about changing plans?' is about adaptability. 'Do you prefer to work alone or with others?' is about team working, so show that you can do both. Keep answers to about twenty or thirty seconds, with a reason.

questions.prompt: For 'What do you do when you have too much to do?', why is 'I make a list, work out what is most urgent and tick things off' stronger than 'I stay calm and get everything done'?

options.text: It is longer, and longer answers earn more marks
It is more modest in tone than the other answer
It is specific and shows how they work
It uses more technical words than the other answer

questions.hint: Specific methods are more convincing than claims.

questions.prompt: Candidate A says 'I'm a planner, always, and I get frustrated by people who do not plan.' What is the main weakness?

options.text: It is too short to be scored properly
It is too modest about the candidate's skills
It does not mention planning at all
It shows rigidity and a negative view of others

questions.hint: The answer suggests low flexibility.

questions.prompt: Why is Candidate B's answer, 'I like to plan, but I am happy to start and adjust', stronger?

options.text: It avoids having to state a preference
It shows flexibility and care for others
It sounds more confident than A's
It is shorter than A's answer

questions.hint: Balanced answers show adaptability.

questions.prompt: Which answer to 'What are you proud of?' is best?

options.text: 'I'm proud of almost everything I have done so far.'
'Helping my nephew learn to read.'
'I try not to boast about anything I have done.'
'I'm proud of being the best person in my team.'

questions.hint: A brief, real example works best.

questions.prompt: What is 'How do you feel about changing plans?' really exploring?

options.text: Preference for routine
Adaptability
Planning skill
Courage

questions.hint: The question is about adaptability.

questions.prompt: What is 'Do you prefer to work alone or with others?' really exploring?

options.text: Team working, so show you can do both
Which kind of office layout you prefer
Whether you hope to become a manager
How much you dislike working in teams

questions.hint: Show flexibility.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long should a strengths answer be?

options.text: A single word with no explanation
About two minutes using the full STAR method
Around five minutes with full background
Around twenty or thirty seconds, with a reason

questions.hint: Short answers with a reason fit strengths questions.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes a strengths answer weak?

options.text: A personal detail
A short reason
Boasting or vagueness
A touch of humour

questions.hint: Weak answers boast or are vague.

questions.prompt: A candidate gives a one-word answer to a strengths question. What would improve it?

options.text: Adding a long story
Repeating the word
Adding a short reason
Asking for the next question

questions.hint: A reason makes the answer meaningful.

questions.prompt: What should you listen for in a strengths question?

options.text: What it is really exploring
The panel's reactions
The first word only
The speed of the question

questions.hint: Understand the intent behind the question.

items.title: Level 5: Probes in practice
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Follow-up questions are where interviews are often decided, so practise them. Imagine you gave this answer: 'A customer was angry about a delay. I listened, apologised, checked the system and gave them a new date.' A probe might be 'What exactly did you say when you apologised?' A strong reply gives the real wording: 'I said, I'm sorry about the delay, I can see how frustrating it must be. Let me check what is going on.' Another probe is 'How did you know the customer was satisfied?' A good reply: 'They thanked me and said they would wait. Later I saw no further complaint.' A weak reply: 'I think they were fine.' Another probe is 'What else could you have done?' A good reply names a realistic alternative and why you did not choose it: 'I could have passed them to my supervisor, but the issue was within my authority and passing it on would have made them wait longer.' Another is 'What was the hardest part?' A good reply is honest: 'Keeping calm when they raised their voice.' A fifth is 'What did you learn?' A good reply is specific: 'I learned to explain next steps before they ask.' Probes often start with 'What', 'How' and 'Why'. Treat them as a chance to show depth, not as an attack. If you do not know the answer, be honest, and say what you remember. Always keep your replies short, then pause to let the panel respond.

questions.prompt: A probe asks 'What exactly did you say when you apologised?' What is the best type of reply?

options.text: The real wording you used
A statement that you are always polite
A summary of your general approach
A description of how the customer reacted

questions.hint: The panel wants specifics.

questions.prompt: A probe asks 'How did you know the customer was satisfied?' Which reply is strongest?

options.text: 'I did not get any feedback from the customer at all.'
'They seemed happy enough when they left the desk.'
'I think they were fine with the outcome in the end.'
'They thanked me and said they would wait.'

questions.hint: Evidence of the outcome is strongest.

questions.prompt: A probe asks 'What else could you have done?' What should your reply include?

options.text: A list of every possible option you could think of
A comment on what your manager should have done
A statement that nothing else was possible
A realistic alternative and why you did not choose it

questions.hint: Show your reasoning.

questions.prompt: A probe asks 'What was the hardest part?' What is the best reply?

options.text: A complaint about how the customer behaved
An honest account of the real difficulty
A joke to lighten the mood
A claim that nothing about it was difficult

questions.hint: Honesty shows reflection.

questions.prompt: A probe asks 'What did you learn?' Which reply is strongest?

options.text: 'I learned that I am good at this kind of work.'
'I learned a great deal from the experience.'
'I learned that customers can be difficult at times.'
'I learned to explain next steps before the customer asks.'

questions.hint: Specific learning is convincing.

questions.prompt: Which words do probes often begin with?

options.text: If, but and because
What, how and why
Who, when and where
Can, will and should

questions.hint: Open questions begin with what, how and why.

questions.prompt: How should you view a probe?

options.text: As a chance to change the subject
As a chance to show depth
As a sign that the answer has failed
As an attack on your honesty

questions.hint: Probes invite more detail.

questions.prompt: How long should a reply to a probe usually be?

options.text: A new full STAR story
Short, followed by a pause
A single word
Over two minutes

questions.hint: Brief replies leave room for more questions.

questions.prompt: If you cannot answer a probe fully, what should you do?

options.text: Ask the panel to skip it
Be honest about what you remember
Change the subject smoothly
Guess confidently

questions.hint: Honesty with what you recall is best.

questions.prompt: Why might a reply such as 'I think they were fine' damage an answer?

options.text: It gives no evidence of the result
It is much too long
It uses the word 'I'
It sounds too formal

questions.hint: A vague outcome weakens the answer.

items.title: Level 5: Confidentiality, honesty and the Civil Service Code in your answers
items.body: Your examples must not break the values that the Civil Service expects. First, confidentiality. If your example comes from a job where you handled personal or sensitive information, do not name customers, patients or pupils. Say, 'a customer' or 'a pupil' instead. Do not reveal details that could identify someone, and do not share private business information from a past employer that is not public. A panel will think well of you for respecting privacy, and badly of you if you share what you should not. Second, honesty. Do not exaggerate your role or claim credit for others' work. If the team achieved something, say what you contributed. Do not describe a result you did not achieve. If you made a mistake, say so. Dishonesty in the application or interview can lead to an offer being withdrawn, and in serious cases to disciplinary action or dismissal if discovered later. Third, impartiality and fairness. Avoid stories where you favoured one person over another without good reason. Avoid expressing strong political opinions, as civil servants serve whichever government is elected, and must be seen to be impartial. Fourth, respect. Do not mock customers or colleagues, even if the story is humorous. Fifth, integrity. A story about doing the right thing when no one was watching, such as reporting an error you made, is attractive. If a question touches on the rules, show that you follow them but also ask for guidance when unsure. These principles apply to your conduct in the interview as well as to your examples.

questions.prompt: In an example about handling a patient's records at a surgery, how should you refer to the patient?

options.text: By their full name, for accuracy
By their initials and age
As 'a patient', with no details
By their first name only

questions.hint: Protect privacy by not identifying people.

questions.prompt: Which of these is it wrong to reveal in an interview?

options.text: Private business information from a past job
Your job title in a previous role
Your own responsibilities in that role
The general type of work you used to do

questions.hint: Confidential information should not be shared.

questions.prompt: What is the right way to describe a team achievement?

options.text: Leave out the result
Say what you contributed to it
Say you were not involved
Claim it as your own work

questions.hint: Be honest about your part.

questions.prompt: What can happen if dishonesty in an application is discovered later?

options.text: A note is added to your file and nothing more
Your salary is reduced for a short time
Nothing, since the job has already been given
An offer can be withdrawn or action taken

questions.hint: Dishonesty has serious consequences.

questions.prompt: Why avoid expressing strong political opinions in the interview?

options.text: Civil servants must be seen to be impartial
The panel will mark you down for any opinion
Opinions can change your pay band
Politics is banned from all workplaces

questions.hint: Impartiality is a core value.

questions.prompt: Which story shows integrity well?

options.text: Winning an argument with a colleague over the best method
Completing a difficult task a day before the deadline
Reporting a mistake you made that no one had noticed
Finding a shortcut that saved the team a lot of time

questions.hint: Integrity includes honest reporting of errors.

questions.prompt: You tell a funny story about a customer's odd behaviour. What is the risk?

options.text: It may confuse the STAR order
It may sound as if you mock customers
It may be about the wrong behaviour
It may be too short to score

questions.hint: Respect is essential.

questions.prompt: How should you respond to a question about following rules?

options.text: Say that rules are not that important
Show that you follow them and ask for guidance when unsure
Say that you make your own rules
Say that you bend rules to get results

questions.hint: Following rules and seeking guidance shows judgement.

questions.prompt: Which of these shows impartiality in an example?

options.text: Treating two customers by the same rules
Leaving a customer who is rude until last
Helping a friend first because you know them
Dealing first with a customer who is nicer

questions.hint: Impartial means the same rules for all.

questions.prompt: Where do these principles apply?

options.text: Only to people with management duties
In your examples and in how you behave in the interview
Only after you have been hired
Only in the examples you choose

questions.hint: Conduct in the interview counts too.

items.title: Level 5: Answering questions about difficult people and conflict
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: Questions about difficult people or conflict are very common, and many candidates handle them poorly by blaming the other person. A strong answer shows maturity. Consider the question 'Tell us about a time you disagreed with a colleague.' A good answer follows a pattern. Name the disagreement briefly: 'A colleague and I disagreed about how to file customer records.' Show you listened: 'I asked her to explain her reasons, and I realised she was worried about missing documents.' Show respect: 'I thanked her for raising it.' Show problem solving: 'We agreed to try her method for a week while I added a check to mine, and then compare.' Show the result: 'Her method was better for urgent items, so we used both depending on the case.' Show learning: 'I learned to ask for reasons before defending my own view.' This pattern also works for difficult customers: acknowledge feelings, listen, clarify, offer what you can do and explain what you cannot, and follow up. Avoid describing the other person as stupid, lazy or unreasonable. Avoid stories where the conflict was solved by someone else, unless you describe your role. Avoid stories in which you simply gave in, as this suggests you may avoid difficult conversations. Also avoid stories in which you won through force. The best conflict stories end with a better relationship or a better process. If the issue was not resolved, you can say so honestly and describe what you did to keep working well. The panel is looking for calm, fairness and respect.

questions.prompt: Why do many candidates handle conflict questions poorly?

options.text: They forget to give a result
They blame the other person
They choose examples that are too recent
They use too many words

questions.hint: Blame signals poor relationships.

questions.prompt: In the model answer, why does asking the colleague to explain her reasons matter?

options.text: It shows you were trying to avoid the problem
It shows you had no view of your own
It shows you needed her permission to act
It shows you listened and understood her concern

questions.hint: Listening is the foundation.

questions.prompt: What does agreeing to try her method for a week show?

options.text: That you wanted to delay a decision
That you disliked your own method
Willingness to test and compare approaches fairly
That you gave in to avoid an argument

questions.hint: It shows problem solving and fairness.

questions.prompt: Why does 'We used both, depending on the case' make a good result?

options.text: It shows the disagreement continued
It avoids having to make a decision
It shows the manager made the decision
It reflects a better process agreed by both

questions.hint: A better process is a strong outcome.

questions.prompt: Which learning statement is strongest?

options.text: 'I learned to ask for reasons before defending my own view.'
'I learned to avoid arguments wherever I can.'
'I learned to speak up more loudly in future.'
'I learned that other people are sometimes wrong.'

questions.hint: Specific, personal learning is convincing.

questions.prompt: How does the same pattern apply to a difficult customer?

options.text: Pass them to a manager as soon as possible
Explain the rules clearly and then end the call
Acknowledge feelings, listen, clarify and follow up
Give them what they ask for in order to calm them

questions.hint: The pattern is empathy, clarity and follow-through.

questions.prompt: Which description of the other person weakens the answer?

options.text: 'She was unreasonable and stubborn.'
'She had more experience of the system.'
'She had a different view.'
'She was worried about missing documents.'

questions.hint: Name-calling suggests a poor attitude.

questions.prompt: Why is a story where you simply gave in a poor choice?

options.text: It is too short to be scored
It suggests you avoid difficult talks
It shows too much flexibility
It shows too much respect

questions.hint: Giving in without discussion looks like avoidance.

questions.prompt: Why is a story where you won through force a poor choice?

options.text: It shows poor respect for others
It lacks a clear result
It is too long to be scored
It has no actions in it

questions.hint: Force harms relationships.

questions.prompt: If the issue was not resolved, what should you do in the answer?

options.text: Change the subject quickly
Blame the other person for the result
Say so honestly and describe how you kept working well
Pretend that it was resolved

questions.hint: Honesty about outcomes is respected.

items.title: Level 5: Closing the interview in different situations
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Behaviours; GOV.UK
items.body: The end of an interview can go in different ways, and you should be ready for each. Suppose the panel asks, 'Do you have any questions for us?' and you have prepared three. Ask one or two, depending on time, and listen to the answers. If the panel seems to be running short of time, ask your most important question and say you have another you can send by email if appropriate. Suppose the panel has already covered all your questions. Say so, and ask something related, such as, 'You mentioned the team is moving to a new system. How will new starters be supported through that?' Suppose the panel's answer raises a concern, for example that the work is more repetitive than you expected. Respond calmly: 'Thank you, that is helpful to know. I enjoy careful, detailed work.' Do not argue or backtrack. Suppose the panel asks, 'Is there anything else you would like to add?' Use it for a short, genuine summary: 'I would just like to say that I am keen on this role because... and I think my experience of... would help.' Keep it to a few sentences. Do not introduce long new stories. Suppose the interview ends abruptly because the panel is late. Thank them and leave politely. If you are told when to expect the result, note it. If not, you can ask. On video, wait until the host ends the call, say goodbye, and click 'Leave'. Afterward, if you remember a significant correction, such as a wrong date, you may contact the recruitment team, though it is rarely necessary.

questions.prompt: You have prepared three questions, but time is short. What is the best approach?

options.text: Ask the panel for more time
Ask all three questions as quickly as you can
Ask your most important question and mention you can follow up if appropriate
Skip your questions completely

questions.hint: Prioritise your best question.

questions.prompt: The panel has already covered all your questions. What can you do?

options.text: Say so and ask a related question
Ask the same questions again to be sure
Ask about the panel's own careers
Say you have none and finish

questions.hint: A related follow-up still shows interest.

questions.prompt: The panel says the work is more repetitive than you expected. What is a good response?

options.text: 'I was told that it would be more varied than that.'
'Could the work be changed to be more varied?'
'That does not sound like what I was hoping for.'
'Thank you, that is helpful. I enjoy detailed work.'

questions.hint: Stay calm and positive.

questions.prompt: The panel asks 'Is there anything else you would like to add?' What is the best use of the chance?

options.text: A request to repeat an earlier answer in full
A new, long story to show another strength
A short, genuine summary of why you want the role
A list of points that you felt went badly

questions.hint: Keep it to a few sentences.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you avoid at the closing stage?

options.text: Thanking the panel
Asking about next steps
Summarising your interest
Introducing a long new story

questions.hint: Long stories do not belong at the end.

questions.prompt: The panel ends the interview abruptly because they are running late. What should you do?

options.text: Mention that the delay was not your fault
Ask them to give you extra time
Thank them and leave politely
Say you have more to add

questions.hint: Politeness leaves a good impression.

questions.prompt: The panel does not say when you will hear the result. What can you ask?

options.text: Who else is being considered
Whether you have done better than the others
What score you were given
When you can expect the result

questions.hint: Asking about timing is reasonable.

questions.prompt: How should you end a video interview?

options.text: Leave before the panel says goodbye
Close the laptop as soon as you finish
Wait for the host to end it, say goodbye and leave
Switch off the camera and stay online

questions.hint: A calm end is best.

questions.prompt: You realise afterwards that you gave a wrong date in an answer. What is a sensible choice?

options.text: Email every panel member to correct it
Consider contacting the recruitment team, though it is rarely necessary
Say nothing, however important it was
Add a correction to your next application

questions.hint: A significant factual correction can be mentioned, but sparingly.

questions.prompt: Why should you not argue or backtrack when the panel mentions a less attractive aspect of the job?

options.text: It shows you have not read the advert
Calm acceptance shows maturity and realism
It lowers your score by itself
It is against the rules of the interview

questions.hint: Handling information calmly shows maturity.

items.title: Level 5: Offers, checks, feedback and next steps in practice
items.body: After the interview, you may face some practical decisions. Suppose you receive a conditional offer but your current employer needs a month's notice. Tell the recruitment team early so the start date can be agreed. Do not hand in your notice until the offer is unconditional. Suppose a referee is slow to respond. Contact them politely, remind them of the deadline, and tell the recruitment team if there is a delay. Suppose you have an old criminal conviction. Many are spent after a set period under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act, and spent convictions generally do not need to be declared for these roles, but unspent ones must be. If you are unsure, ask the vetting team, and be honest. Suppose you have lived abroad and cannot provide references from the whole period. Explain the situation and ask what alternatives are acceptable. Suppose you are placed on a reserve list. Keep your details up to date, continue applying elsewhere, and reply promptly if contacted. Suppose you receive feedback saying that your examples lacked detail on your actions. Rewrite your stories in STAR form with three or four clear actions, practise aloud, and apply for similar roles. Suppose you are rejected and you think the process was unfair. Ask for feedback first, then if you still have concerns, follow the department's complaints process, and, if needed, the Civil Service Commission. Suppose you get two offers. Ask each team for a reasonable time to decide, and be honest with both. Whatever happens, thank the team for their time.

questions.prompt: Your current employer needs a month's notice. What is the best step after receiving a conditional offer?

options.text: Tell the recruitment team early about the notice
Hand in your notice immediately to start the clock
Ignore the notice period and agree to start at once
Ask the team to start you the next day

questions.hint: Early information helps plan a realistic start date.

questions.prompt: A referee is slow to respond. What should you do?

options.text: Write the reference yourself and send it in
Name a different referee without telling anyone
Withdraw the application to avoid delay
Chase them politely and tell the team

questions.hint: Keep the team informed.

questions.prompt: What is the rule about unspent convictions for roles requiring BPSS?

options.text: They must be declared
They are declared only after the offer
Only the serious ones need declaring
They never need to be declared

questions.hint: Unspent convictions must be declared.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether a conviction is spent. What should you do?

options.text: Ask a friend what they think
Ask the vetting team and be honest
Wait to see if it is checked
Leave it out to avoid trouble

questions.hint: Seek advice and be honest.

questions.prompt: You lived abroad and cannot provide references for the whole period. What is the best approach?

options.text: Provide made-up references to fill the gap
Explain the situation and ask what alternatives are acceptable
Withdraw from the process altogether
Leave that part of your history blank

questions.hint: Ask for acceptable alternatives.

questions.prompt: You are on a reserve list. Which behaviour is most sensible?

options.text: Keep details current and reply quickly
Stop applying elsewhere and wait for the offer
Wait for the team to find you if you move
Contact the team daily to check on progress

questions.hint: Stay available and active.

questions.prompt: Feedback says your examples lacked detail on your actions. What is the best response?

options.text: Add more background to each of your stories
Rewrite stories with clear actions
Avoid behaviour questions in future interviews
Choose shorter stories for each question

questions.hint: Fix the weak part directly.

questions.prompt: You think the process was unfair. What should you do first?

options.text: Reapply immediately for the same job
Write to a minister about the process
Ask for feedback, then complain formally
Post a complaint publicly on social media

questions.hint: Follow the formal route.

questions.prompt: You receive two job offers. What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Ignore one until the other is confirmed
Accept both and decide later
Tell each team that the other offer has been refused
Ask each team for time and be honest with both

questions.hint: Be honest and communicate.

questions.prompt: Why is it worth thanking the team even if you are rejected?

options.text: It leaves a good impression
It may change the decision
It is required by the Civil Service Code
It earns bonus points on later applications

questions.hint: Professional courtesy helps your reputation.
